column2: Call the Great Hunt

Sound the horns and call every chieftain of the herd to the Great Hunt. For two months the warherd sweeps the deep forest in a great ring, driving stag, boar and the men of the woodland villages towards the herdstone, where you take the first kill. The herd that hunts together remembers who leads it.
The horns sound for the Great Hunt.\n
[Root.GetTitledName] called the Great Hunt at [Root.Location.GetName].
Fervour of the Great Hunt
Called the Great Hunt
Locked horns in the Great Hunt
Beaten in the Great Hunt
Every chieftain of your herd fit to hunt must come.
You lead your warriors into the forest to take your place in the ring.
You take the first kill, then the chieftains take theirs.
You lower your horns and charge into the trapped quarry.
The razorgor runt is penned beside your seat.
Your razorgor is butchered.
Your razorgor goes back to the forest.
Your razorgor stays in its pen.
Your razorgor is dead.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] has you beaten before the herd.

You put the great horn to your lips and its bellow rolls out over the treetops, and from glade and gully the horns of your chieftains answer it. The summer is ending and the forest is fat with game: it is time for the Great Hunt. Your gors will spread out in a ring many leagues wide and drive everything that runs before them, stag and boar and wolf and the soft men of the woodcutters' villages, until the ring closes at the herdstone and you take the first kill.
Now we shall see who in this herd is strong.

The horn of [From.GetTitledFirstName] has sounded over the forest: the Great Hunt is called, and every chieftain must answer it. You gather your gors and ungors and go to take your place in the ring. Those who are slow, or who break the line, will be remembered.
To the hunt!

You were driving your ungors through a thicket of thorn when a great boar burst from its wallow and drove its tusks into your thigh before you could get your horns down. Your warriors finished it with their spears, but your leg is torn open and the blood will not stop. The hunt is over for you.
Curse the beast!
Word comes down the ring that [From.GetTitledFirstName] has been gored by a boar and carried from the hunt with a torn leg.
The forest takes the weak.

Your warriors and those of [herdhunt_rival.GetTitledFirstName] came together at a stream and both of you claimed the ground nearer the herdstone. Neither would give way. Before both warbands you lowered your horns and charged, and the two of you fought until your gors dragged you apart, bloody and snorting. It is not over.

Your warriors and those of [herdhunt_brawler.GetTitledFirstName] came together at a stream and [herdhunt_brawler.GetFirstName] claimed the ground nearer the herdstone. You would not give way. Before both warbands [herdhunt_brawler.GetFirstName] lowered [herdhunt_brawler.GetHerHis] horns and charged you, and the two of you fought until your gors dragged you apart, bloody and snorting. It is not over.
One day I will have those horns.

[herdhunt_brawler.GetTitledFirstName] and [herdhunt_rival.GetTitledFirstName] fought over who would stand nearer the herdstone, horn to horn before their warbands, and had to be dragged apart. Neither will forget it. So it is in every herd: each one watches the one above him, and waits.
Let them fight. The strongest will rise.

Your ungors were slow and lazy in the thickets, and a gap opened in your stretch of the ring. Who can say how much of the quarry slipped through? A herd of stags at least, and some of the villagers too. When [From.GetTitledFirstName] hears of it, there will be a reckoning.

As you drove your warriors through the trees a great stag stepped into the glade before you, and before you could think your spear was in its heart. It is a fine beast, but no blood may be shed before the first kill at the herdstone, and that kill belongs to [From.GetTitledFirstName]. Your gors are already whispering.
There will be trouble for this.

Through sloth or weakness, [From.GetTitledFirstName] let a gap open in the ring, and much of the quarry has escaped. The herd watches to see what you will do: a chieftain who shames the hunt is beaten before the herd. Let it pass, and others may think you grow soft.

[From.GetTitledFirstName] has killed a stag before the first kill at the herdstone, taking blood that was yours by right. The herd watches to see what you will do: a chieftain who steals the Beastlord's kill is beaten before the herd. Let it pass, and others may think you grow soft.
Beat [From.GetHerHim] bloody before them all!
Let it pass this time.

[From.GetTitledFirstName] had you dragged before the herd and beaten with spear shafts until you could not stand, while your own warriors looked on. You will carry the marks for a long time, and so will your pride.
I will remember this.

The ring has closed. Into the clearing before the herdstone your warherd has driven a bellowing, screaming mass of stags, boars, wolves and the men of the villages, packed so tight that they trample one another. Every eye in the herd is on you, for the first kill is yours alone. Only when you have taken it may the chieftains take theirs.
Blood for the herdstone!
[From.GetTitledFirstName] has taken the first kill at the herdstone and the horns sound again: now it is the turn of the chieftains. The trapped quarry mills in terror before you.
Mine!

You were magnificent in the killing ground. Your spear found a great stag and a boar, and you brought down two of the fleeing men with your bare hands. All the herd saw it, and your warriors bray your name.
Let them remember who hunts best!

One young gor stood out in the hunt above all the rest. He held his stretch of the ring alone when the ungors beside him fled, brought down a boar with his bare hands and threw two older gors into the stream when they tried to take it from him. His horns are already thick. Your bray-shaman says the Dark Gods have marked him for a wargor.
Bring him to my side.
Let him prove himself in the warherd first.

When the ring closed it caught a sounder of razorgors, great tusked brutes with hides like bark and tempers like fire. They have gored three ungors already, and the herders have them penned with spears. Among them is a runt with bristles the colour of rust that charges anyone who comes near the pen. The beasts are yours to do with as you wish.
I will keep the runt.
Yoke them all for war!
Roast them for the feast!

The killing is done, but some of the men of the villages are still alive, huddled in the trampled clearing. Your old gors say that a few should be let run, so they can tell the other villages what waits in the forest, and men will fear it all the more. But the herdstone is thirsty, and the Dark Gods love the blood of men.
Let them run and tell the others.
Drag them all to the herdstone!

Great fires burn around the herdstone and the carcasses turn on spits. Skins of wine and of stranger brews taken from the villages are passed from hand to hand. The hunt is over, and the herd will feast until there is nothing left.
Feast, my herd!
Meat and wine!

The fires are burned down and only bones are left around the herdstone. The chieftains lead their warriors back to their own lairs, fat and proud and full of the hunt. It will be some years before the game returns to these woods and the villages dare to send their woodcutters out again, but when they do, your horn will sound once more.
The fires are burned down and only bones are left around the herdstone. You gather your warriors and go back to your own lair, fat and proud and full of the hunt.
A good hunt.

Messengers have come running through the forest: war has come to your lands! There is no time to finish the hunt now. Your horns sound the recall, the ring breaks apart, and the chieftains lead their warriors away to fight.
The horns of [From.GetTitledFirstName] are sounding the recall: war has come, and the Great Hunt is over before the ring could close.
There will be other prey.

The chieftains of a neighbouring herd have come to your lair, and the first thing they saw was your razorgor, grown huge and terrible, straining at its chains and snapping at them as they passed. They gave it a wide berth, and they spoke to you with a great deal more respect after that.
It knows its master, and so should they.

Your razorgor broke loose from its pen this morning and charged straight at [herdhunt_victim.GetTitledFirstName], who was too slow to get out of its way. The beast's tusks laid [herdhunt_victim.GetHerHis] side open before the herders could drag it off.

Your razorgor broke loose from its pen this morning and charged straight at [herdhunt_victim.GetTitledFirstName], who was too slow to get out of its way. The beast trampled [herdhunt_victim.GetHerHim] into the mud and savaged [herdhunt_victim.GetHerHis] limbs. [herdhunt_victim.GetSheHeCap] will live, but never whole.

Your razorgor broke loose from its pen this morning and charged straight at [herdhunt_victim.GetTitledFirstName], who was too slow to get out of its way. By the time the herders dragged the beast off, there was not much left of [herdhunt_victim.GetFirstName].
It is a beast. It does what beasts do.
Butcher the brute.

Your razorgor has stopped eating. It lies in its pen all day with its snout to the bars, facing the forest, and grunts at no one. The herders say it hears the sounders calling in the deep woods. Perhaps it is time to let it go.
Go then, back to the forest.
It stays. It is mine.
Your razorgor was found dead in its pen this morning, its great bulk cold and still. It had grown old and heavy. The herd will eat it in your honour, as is fitting.
It was a fine beast.
